questions.prompt: Why start a change on a branch rather than committing straight to main?
choices: Branches make commits faster
Work stays separate from the current state of the project until it is ready
main cannot accept commits
Only branches can be reviewed
questions.explain: A branch keeps unfinished work away from the branch everyone treats as current, which also gives CI something to check before a merge.

questions.prompt: A pipeline run failed. Which two facts identify what it ran against?
choices: The repository name and the author
The commit and the branch
The runner and the operating system
The workflow name and the time
questions.explain: A run happens against a specific commit on a specific branch. Small commits make that answer useful.

choices: A copy of the repository
A pointer at the newest commit in a line of commits
A folder inside .github
A snapshot of the working directory
questions.explain: A branch is a moving pointer at a commit. That is why creating one is cheap.

questions.prompt: Where does a pipeline report its result on a pull request?
choices: The Conversation tab
The Checks tab
The Files changed tab
The Commits tab
questions.explain: Checks shows the results of automated tests, builds, and scans for the proposed changes.

questions.prompt: A reviewer selects Request changes. What happens?
choices: The pull request is closed
The merge is blocked until it is resolved
The branch is deleted
The checks re-run
questions.explain: Requesting changes blocks the merge deliberately, until someone resolves or dismisses it.

questions.prompt: What does a green check tell you that an approval does not?
choices: That a person read the change
That the automated tests ran and passed
That the branch is up to date
That the change is safe to deploy
questions.explain: Approval says a person looked. A check says the automation ran. They answer different questions, so teams usually want both.

questions.prompt: When is a fork the right choice instead of a branch?
choices: When the change is large
When you do not have write access to the repository
When you want the change reviewed
When the repository is private
questions.explain: A fork is your own repository, which is what lets you propose changes to a project you cannot write to.

choices: The original repository your fork was copied from
The default branch of your fork
A mirror on another host
The repository that runs the pipeline
questions.explain: Your fork stays connected to the upstream repository, which is how pull requests can flow back.

questions.prompt: Why do pull requests from forks need care in a pipeline?
choices: They run slower
They propose code that is not yours, so the workflow must not hand it secrets
They cannot be reviewed
They always target the default branch
questions.explain: The proposing code comes from outside the project. The security module covers exactly how the triggers differ.

questions.prompt: Which ruleset rule makes a CI check binding rather than advisory?
choices: Block force pushes
Require status checks to pass before merging
Restrict deletions
Require linear history
questions.explain: Requiring status checks is what stops the merge until your pipeline reports green.

questions.prompt: What does a strict required status check add, compared with a loose one?
choices: It runs more checks in parallel
The branch must be up to date with the base branch before merging
It requires an approving review as well
It blocks force pushes
questions.explain: Strict means re-running against the updated base, which costs builds but avoids merging against a stale base.

questions.prompt: Can rulesets and older branch protection rules both apply to one branch?
choices: No, a ruleset replaces them
Yes, and all applicable rules are enforced
Only if the ruleset is disabled
Only for tags
questions.explain: They work alongside each other and every applicable rule is enforced.

questions.prompt: Why does 'require a pull request before merging' not guarantee a review?
choices: Reviews are always optional on GitHub
The rule requires a pull request to be opened, not approved, unless you also require approvals
It only applies to forks
It applies to tags, not branches
questions.explain: On its own the rule requires the pull request to exist. Requiring a number of approving reviews is a separate setting.
